title: Capsular specificity in temperate phages of Klebsiella pneumoniae is driven by diverse receptor-binding enzymes
experiments_summary: The study combined large-scale genomic, computational, and experimental approaches. (1) Genome dataset assembly: 3,900 Klebsiella genomes from two curated collections (KASPAH: 391 clinical isolates from Melbourne; KLEBPAVIA: 3,509 One Health isolates from Italy) were assembled, with 99 KASPAH genomes additionally sequenced by Oxford Nanopore to produce hybrid assemblies (KASPAH-REF). (2) Bacterial typing: Capsular loci (K-loci) were predicted with Kaptive/Kleborate, and bacterial isolates were grouped into sequence clusters (SCs) using PopPunk to control for population structure. Species were classified using Kleborate, and a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was built from core-gene SNPs using IQ-TREE. (3) Prophage prediction: Prophages were identified using VirSorter, PhiSpy, and CheckV in 2,527 genomes with confident K-locus assignments, retaining regions with ≥50% completeness and ≥2 kb length, yielding 8,105 prophage regions. (4) Prophage annotation: ORFs were predicted with prodigal-gv and clustered with MMseqs2. Clusters were functionally annotated by HHblits searches against PHROGs and ECOD databases. (5) GWAS: An elastic-net regression (via pyseer) was applied to correlate presence/absence of prophage protein clusters (PC50) with K-locus assignments across 35 K-loci, using SCs as covariates. Six clustering thresholds (combinations of 50%/80% identity and 50%/80% coverage) were tested. Predictor performance was evaluated by precision, recall, F1 score, MCC, and bootstrap confidence intervals. (6) Structural modeling: Representative proteins from top GWAS predictors were modeled in 3D using AlphaFold3, and domain architectures were mapped using ECOD classifications; non-RBP predictors were further searched against CATH, PDB, and AlphaFold databases with FoldSeek. (7) Manual depolymerase curation (KASPAH-REF): Starting from 469 prophage proteins (≥500 aa, annotated as tail fiber/spike, containing lyase or hydrolase domains), 124 sequence clusters were formed. Representatives were modeled with AlphaFold2 and screened for parallel β-helix folds, yielding 50 candidates from 32 clusters for recombinant expression. (8) Recombinant protein expression and purification: Candidate genes were cloned into pET101 with C-terminal His-tags and expressed in E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) under standard (1 mM IPTG, 18°C) and alternative (0.5 mM IPTG, 15°C) conditions; proteins were purified using His-tag pulldown and analyzed by SDS-PAGE. For eight non-expressing candidates, a systematic re-expression campaign varied IPTG concentration, temperature, culture density, and duration. Selected proteins predicted by GWAS were commercially synthesized (codon-optimized), cloned into pET30a with N-terminal His-tags, and produced by GenScript. (9) Enzymatic activity screening: Spot assays on TSA plates were performed by spotting crude lysates and purified proteins onto lawns of 128 Klebsiella strains representing 118 K-types; halo formation was assessed after overnight incubation at 37°C plus 24 h at room temperature. Minimal halo-forming concentrations (MHFCs) were determined. (10) SGNH hydrolase activity assays: Two GWAS-predicted SGNH-domain tail fibers (164_08-KL2 and 174_38-KL55) and one β-helix depolymerase negative control (184_43-KL111) were tested using a spectrophotometric p-nitrophenyl acetate (pNPA) hydrolysis assay (405 nm, 20 min, 96-well format, 10 µg protein, 100 µM pNPA, 25°C) with 2 biological × 3 technical replicates. A complementary phenol-red pH-shift assay (0.002% phenol red, measured at 560 nm) was used to confirm acetic acid release. (11) ECOD domain prevalence analysis: ECOD domain distributions across 4,598 high-completeness prophages were analyzed for RBP-annotated protein clusters, and K-locus diversity per cluster was quantified using the Simpson index to assess capsule-specificity of different domain families.
